newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian banks still await revival of credit demand.
newsitem.headline: Indian banks still await revival of credit demand.

text.p: Hopes of revived demand for Indian bank credit could be misplaced with money conditions expected to remain tight in coming months, bankers and analysts said on Thursday.

The chairman of the State Bank of India, India's largest commercial bank, said last week demand for credit was picking up, but top officials of several other banks said they had yet to see any signs of that.
"Compared to last year, the demand for credit is lower," said P.H. Ravikumar, vice president of ICICI Bank.
He said a fall in interest rates might stimulate industrial activity and demand for credit. "But it's dull right now."
SBI cut its prime lending rate by half a percentage point to 15.5 percent a year on September 6 to stimulate demand.

"The latest figures released by Reserve Bank of India (RBI) don't support the statement that demand for credit is picking up," Aashish Pitale, manager, debt research at ICICI Securities and Finance Company, said.

"For long-term funds there should be demand but for short-term funds, the demand would be less," said B.N. Puranmalka, managing director of leading fertiliser firm Indo Gulf Fertilisers and Chemicals Corporation.
"Virtually every treasury is saying credit pickup is slow," said the treasurer of a European bank in Bombay. "I get the impression that companies are consciously downsizing."

The imposition of a minimum tax on companies in India's 1996/97 budget in July -- which removed the tax shelter previously available on large capital investments -- had dampened investment enthusiasm, he said.
"Last year was a good year for credit," said Prabodh Agarwal, banking analyst at securities firm James Capel B&K.
"This year it has been slow to pick up. It should pick up now, but the growth may not be high because of the industrial slowdown."
Agarwal said cuts in prime lending rates were not likely to lead to a substantial increase in credit offtake.
"Growth (in credit) would come irrespective of it, if there is enough commercial activity," he said.
India's leading industry associations said fiscal 1995/96 (April-March) was characterised by a liquidity crunch which had led to a slowdown in industrial production.
Crosby Securities said this month it expected credit creation by Indian banks to pick up in October on the back of an industrial revival.
S. Venkitaramanan, former RBI governor, told Reuters last week he expected industrial activity to pick up in the busy season (October to April).
"Demand for credit will rise and even short-term (interest) rates will go up," he said.
